title: MASSIVE CHALICE
text: TLDR it looks nice, it plays fairly well, and it's unforgiving on the easiest level.  Think niche XCOM. It's a good game but it is missing a few things that seem to me to be odd ... first off, there is no option for any of the characters to 'hold' their action until something comes into range / sight.  Either you attack it on your turn or you don't at all ... there's no 'overwatch'.  Further, it's not clear what the ranges of various non-melee weapons are, so it's hard to tell if, when you move to a location, whether or not you'll be able to hit something.  Finally, it keeps the camera at a 45 degree angle and rotates 90 degrees from there, but some actions, like Charge, can be performed on all 8 compass points, so it's hard to line things up.  Finally, even on Regular mode, the game is unforgiving and sometimes feels like the RNG gods just have it out for you. I wish there was more of a choice as to which heroes were involved with which events, so you could send a promising young character out on a quest rather than it seemingly randomly picking a hero for you to use. Graphically it has a beautiful style, both in combat and between combats, and it doesn't take too long to play through the full 300 year campaign.

title: MASSIVE CHALICE
text: It's a great concept for a game. The idea is a tactical turn based strategy game that is drawn out over generations. So you don't simply manage a squad of heroes, but rather a dynasty and genealogy that you have to develop overy many years in order to breed great leaders and fighters for you to combat this ever-present demonic army threat. As such, many of the threats you will face are not simply the battles but rather the slow passage of time, and the random events that can either benefit you or lose your heroes. I find it very difficult and deeply frustrating but at the same time, I enjoy how involved it is. It brings other elements of strategy into the mix that regular games don't. There's a bunch of small nitpicky things that bother me about it, but it's a good experience overall. If you're a strategy fan, it's definitely worth checking out.

title: MASSIVE CHALICE
text: Right, this one gets a cautious recommendation, mostly because of the combat. Also, points for being one of a few Early Access games that's actually complete, but just needs more content (you know, the way it's supposed to be). Story: the story is, you are a god-like entity brought into being by the Massive Chalice to save the lands from the encroaching Cadence, which you will do over the stretch of three hundred years. I liked the dual voices of the Massive Chalice, and there's nothing to really complain about on that front. Gameplay: You control different houses, and attempt to keep the bloodlines going throughout the three hundred years required for the chalice to activate while fighting off occasional incursions and doing research to improve the lands/heroes. It's a very good system, and the moment the game gave me a character in the Armstrong lineage named "Alex-Louis", the idea of passing down his Alchemist technique through the Armstrong line for generations never stopped being funny. The rub (and indeed, the caution part of this tale) is in the combat. This game most clearly takes influence from XCOM: Enemy Unknown and (to a lesser extent) Fire Emblem: Awakening. Problem is, it lacks the balance of the former, the insane depth of the latter and the expediency of both. One of the things I liked about those games (I'm using them for comparison because it's exactly the same turn-based combat XCOM was) is that you could move through a turn quickly. You could immediately end your turn in both games if people still had moves left but you were satisfied with your position. You could tailor FE:A to move through combat and turns quick, and you could switch to other people in XCOM while a squadmate was still executing his/her turn. It kept the game from being too slow, and I feel like this combat lacks it.It's also not helped by the characters taking strangely wonky path that would sometimes do a near 360 to get to a box when they could just step four paces in a straight line. Also, I despise how the camera would linger on an enemy after you miss, as if to congratulate you on an unlucky dice roll and slow the pace down further. On top of that, the balance was fine right up until I hit the Bulwarks, which I felt were introduced long before I had the capability to deal with them. It kept going on like that from there. Also, like XCOM, the game has a fog of war which the enemies aren't supposed to hit you from until you find each other. Problem is, some of the enemies don't obey that rule, and I'd keep getting hit by ranged units that'd come flying out of the fog of war with (metaphorical) guns blazing even though I hadn't discovered them yet. Also, do you remember how you'd kinda chuckle in XCOM when it'd say you had a 95% chance to hit and you'd still miss like...1 out of every 8-10 shots? Enjoy the most deceptive percentage system in history, where 90% means you're gonna miss 2-3 out of every 5 shots. At one point, out of curiosity, I actually reloaded a save to see how many times I hit an enemy I had an 80% shot of hitting. I got 12 out of 20 before I stopped. Maybe I got unlucky, but that actually feels like a very accurate representation of the accuracy in this game. I understand it's gamblers fallacy to assume 80% means I'll hit four out of five times, but there's a massive difference between that and a near constant 50%. Which leads to the chief complaint about the combat system: its ambiguity. I have to guesstimate how far the enemies are going to move, the percentage system lies to me, caberjacks never seem to be close enough to help anything, and there are the glancing blows that are the RNG's way of saying "you're not appreciating this combat system enough, allow me to screw you over because the unreliable hit percentage wasn't enough." The entire point of strategy and tactics is that a game should do more or less what you tell it, with a little room for surprises. If something goes wrong, it should be because I took a chance and it didn't pay off, and hopefully I'll have enough options to compensate for that. It shouldn't be because the system is so unreliable that I have no idea whether my tactics will work or not. It desperately needs refinement, is what I'm saying. Still, the generations system is awesome, and makes the game worth playing, and for all its frustrations, the combat system has its moments.

title: MASSIVE CHALICE
text: Wonderful little game of the XCOM meets Banner Saga' and Rogue Legacy' ideas vein. Nothing of a large scale here, just a 700 meg game that nevertheless does everything right. The tactics' are there, the artwork is finest, the oft times fun narration and (end theme) story are awesome, moving, and in a sense allegorical. Little random events here and there add flavour and variability. There's also an overarching feel of progression, plus challenge. Chalice is a grower though, its "indieness" can be off-putting at first. It has also been said for cons that characters in the game die so often (of age) that you can't remember them nor form any connection. That's somewhat true, yet I think it holds separate value that only a flag and its legacy will stay visible, this theme also supports the end-story. Could have done with some more city building and strategy, maybe more story elements. You know, more content. Yet for this size and this price, there's plenty of fun and wonder here. It plays perfectly well, not like XCOM 2 (which is unplayable on many systems and terribly optimized, for little to no merit). This one actually looks artistic. Has more 'soul'. Massive Chalice is a well done game that I'm more than happy I've played.

title: MASSIVE CHALICE
text: I don't know where to start. Massive Chalice is probably one of the best games I've ever played. It's so amazing how much story you can get on just a simple premise. The story ends up being as procedurally generated as all the other elements of the game. If you play in a way to just let things happen, then you end up with an amazing and unique story that spans multiple generations of multiple family lines combating a common enemy. Things don't go to plan sometimes and that just adds to the beauty of it. You planned for someone in your party to marry another? Well he dies when another party member accidentally throws a bomb on him. Then you have to find another suitor. But then they still end up with an amazing family line. That war veteran who battled the Cadence whom retired and had children? Well, the cadence attacks their castle in their old age! But wait! Due to their experience in battle, they fight honorably against overwhelming odds! Brother can fight alongside brother. Mother can fight alongside daughter. Even grandpa can get into the fray! The randomized traits and personalities also add spice to the mix. This family line produces offspring that are each strong as an ox? Well, they might all be prone to depression. That wise old master you have teaching all your young heroes? Well he might be an alcoholic and you created a whole generation of drunkards. And don't get me started on the philosophy. You effectively play as a god for a span of 300 years. You care about these people and you see them be born, fight, and eventually mourn their passing, but their legacy lives on! Whether you believe in a god or not, it certainly makes you think about what it's like to be one, the effects of decisions, cause and effect, control, how much omnipotence does a god actually have when you factor in free will and randomness? Does a god actually care? Are some people more favoured over others? This game also gives you a big picture look at life. It changed my perspectives and pre-conceived notions. Aren't we all expected to grow up, contribute to society, get married, and have children? But the reality is that not everyone will live that life, whether by circumstances or by choice. But whether or not you end up living that life, you can still contribute greatly to society. Some of my greatest heroes in this game never had children. Some go on to mentor others, and in a sense carry on their legacy that way. You don't have to get married and have children to be great or to have epic stories told about you or continue your legacy. Some will die too young, some will live long lives. Some will have boring lives, some will have amazing lives. Even if you lived a boring life, did it still have meaning? Imagine being chosen for something, in this case being able to fight the Cadence. You are able to do this thing that not many are able to do. You have trained to do this thing. It is your speciality. Yet, the when the opportunity comes to show what you're made of, you were never chosen. You never got to do anything. This was the fate of some of the characters. They never got the chance to fight. They never got the chance to have a family. They never got the chance to teach others. How many people in the world today live this kind of life? Did it still have meaning? It's quite sobering to think of this. The narrations by the Chalice's two personalities were entertaining throughout the epic saga. The random small story popups were sometimes hilarious and refreshing. As the game progresses, the stakes keep getting higher, and culminate in a final thrilling battle, and the revelation at the end was just spinechilling. Although the graphics weren't that great, it had a certain charm. The music was amazing. The gameplay was exhilarating and fun. I only wished that I could have recorded it all so that I can revisit the stories and my decisions anytime in the future. As of now, they are fated to disappear with time. Definitely 10/10

title: Mafia II
text: 5/10 Average NOTE: THIS REVIEW CONTAINS MAJOR SPOILERS Here is Mafia 2 in a nutshell: 3 hours of cutscenes, 4 hours of driving, an hour and ahalf of walking around in missions, and another hour and ahalf of shooting. Pros: - Graphics on high settings are fantastic. facial animations during in-game cut scenes are incredible. - Voice acting is very well done. - Cover-based-shooting is solid and gritty. - Some really great characters - SPOILER: ------->Joe's fat♥♥♥♥♥dies at the end. Cons: - An Open world with nothing to do outside the main story. Why is this a problem? Because all you will be doing is driving from your house to your friends house, you and your friend will go do the mission, you then have to drive your friend back to his house, and then you drive back to your place. Driving takes up the majority of gameplay. - Lack of Radio stations: You only have 3 stations with the same 5 songs on each station, and since the majority of the game is driving, it becomes old real fast. Why not also have folk/jazz/country stations? - The story is presented in a way that fits an open world style game with alot of stuff to do. transitioning from one mission to the next is awkward because the story moves to fast and things just get lost in the mix. - Terrible checkpoint system. - You can drag dead bodies which serves no purpose - you can open your trunk which serves no purpose( why not have it to store guns? why must vito be able to carry 7 guns and grenades at once?) - The NPC's are completely lifeless, the city feels barren and empty. - SPOILER-------------->Joe is annoying and i'm surprised he lived as long as he did in the game. I got sick and tired of hearing "I'm the best!" and "You shoot like my sister" for the 1000th time in combat. - SPOILER:------------->Alot of wasted opportunities to explore vitos past and the relationship with his family. The part when Vito found out his father was actually murdered all those years ago was so rushed and pooly done that it was embarrassing - Money is absolutely pointless in the game. - Upgrading cars is pointless. I upgraded a car then went to do a mission, next thing I know when the mission is over my car was nowhere to be found. - There is an absurd amount of cops in this game which really slows down the experience. It's not fun outrunning or engaging them. They are a nuisance, plain and simple. Literally a cop every 2 blocks. - Your car can run out of gas. This feature belongs in a game with alot more content, not a linear open world game with nothing to do but the main story. I hate to rag on this game, but it deserves it, especially after researching and finding out how much the developers left out for release.

title: Mafia II
text: I'm actually a bit split whether to recommend this game or not, but I ended up as you see recommending it. I followed this game a lot running up to its release and I ended up being both disappointed and not... The game should have been longer regarding its story and ambitions. Running towards the end of the game it just felt rushed, like it had to be wrapped up which is a damn shame. The story got both ups and downs, and I would be lying if I said it did not grip me at some point. It's well written but it's everything leading up to the ending and the ending itself that kills it. It still looks great if you ask me. The only thing that disappointed me when it comes to graphics is the damage on cars is not anywhere near the quality of GTA IV which came out 2 years earlier. The gameplay is pretty good and you're punished if you go for a run and gun tactic. The soundtrack for this game is also one of the best I've ever heard in a game. Outside the story there's not much for you to do in this open world and that takes away from the experience as well. But if all these things are taken under consideration, then the next game, if there's going to be one could be amazing! Nevertheless it's a really good experience that I would recommend you if you like me, are fascinated by the mafia.

title: Mafia III
text: Mafia 3 is a wonderful storytelling experience that steeps the player into the culture of the 1960s and 1970s.  From start to finish the story remains engaging and complelling with event beats that create a wonderful pace based on the player's own behavior as they proceed through quests and story events. Every character that you meet going through this world is as interesting and diverse as the setting. So much I believe that the supporting character of Jack Donovan was a scene stealer with every interaction that the story brought him into. And for those interested in how Mafia 2's story plays out for its own protagonist will find some great answers here. The biggest help for this immersion is the music of the era. Everywhere you go there are radios, jukeboxes, and even car radios that can be listened to that provide music from known artists from that era. One moment you could be mixing it up with Creedence Clearwater's Bad Moon Rising then kicking a station over to Aretha Franklin's Rrespect. All interweaved with talk radio and advertisements representative of the game's local color. The gameplay for Mafia 3 is similar to other entries into the franchise, in that it too fits the semi-open world over the shoulder third person view of other games like Grand Theft Auto and Assassin's Creed. This can make gun combat difficult at times since a lot of the game uses a cover/stealth mechanic and the use of pseudo-aim down the barrel method that can make lining up shots difficult. Otherwise this means combat is succinct and brutal on the hard settings for those who love a good challenge. Graphically the game shows its age as it seems to rely upon the same technology used to make Mafia 2. The cutscenes were detailed but in some cases were overshadowed by the lack of good texturing or just bad resolution. And this came through in many of the game models out in the world. There also seemed to be a few persistent bugs that required a full reboot of the game - such as the furniture in diners being relocated completely outside the store as if the models were incorrectly placed, or the minimap and ability to interface with objects and people disappearing. This could become quite frustrating when trying to complete mission objectives or interact with vital NPCs to forward the story along. In the end I recommend Mafia 3 for the great soundtrack and storytelling experience. Fans of Mafia 2 will enjoy Mafia 3 because it continues the quality they've come to expect and new entries will be introduced to the best story in the franchise so far.
